summary:
Manisa falls under Turkey's national legal and security framework. The sources behind this record contain no statute, incident, police action or court decision specific to Manisa, so a trans visitor's exposure in this province is the national position. The nearest named provincial action is in İzmir, where a court ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved in December 2025.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility conditions and government-approved hospital evaluation, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three years. The package is national legislation and would apply in Manisa on enactment.

The baseline law is more permissive than the drafting. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military.

Enforcement against assembly and expression has been sustained. Since 2015 Turkish authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, that three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were continuing at year's end. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49.

Care access tightened during 2025. In June 2025 Turkey's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but none were ultimately submitted to parliament.

Two further developments are recorded for 2026. A February 2026 press report described legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; that measure was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.
tangentialFactors:
The October 2025 reporting on the 11th Judicial Package and Amnesty's account of three draft packages in 2025 describe the same legislative direction: the drafts were prepared and publicised, and at the points reported none had been enacted. Conduct that the drafts would criminalise is not itself an offence under current Turkish law.

The Erdoğan government's stated framing of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' recurs across the sources, including the İzmir court's December 2025 reasoning that the Young LGBTI+'s images were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and the naming of the September 2026 'My Family is Safe' raids. That framing is the common thread linking judicial, police and administrative action.

Decriminalisation since 1858 and legal gender recognition since 1888-set precedent place Turkey above several regional peers on paper, while the ILGA-Europe 2026 Rainbow ranking of 47th of 49 measures the lived gap between statute and enforcement. Istanbul, where most documented enforcement occurs, is a long distance from Manisa, but the legal instruments cited are national.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Turkey have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and marriage eligibility follows the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a legally recognised gender change alters whom a person may marry. The 11th Judicial Package as reported would make that process far harder, raising the care age to 25 and adding infertility and government-approved hospital conditions.

No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no general statutory claim in employment, housing, health or education. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service.

Associations face dissolution and coordinated raids. A İzmir court ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved in December 2025 over 'obscene' images, and the September 2026 'My Family is Safe' operation targeted 9 associations and 13 businesses alongside 162 suspects. Residents taking part in pride events since 2015 have encountered bans, tear gas, water cannon, mass detention and, in 2025, continuing prosecutions of 92 people in Istanbul.

Hormone supply for people under 21 has been banned by the medicines agency since June 2025 despite the statutory access age of 18, restricting transition-related care for younger residents regardless of any pending legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Manisa-specific statute, police practice, incident or court decision appears in the sourced material; the province is represented here only through national law. Whether GBT-style identity checks, pride bans or association operations have been carried out in Manisa is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The enactment status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved in the sources: Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025, and Amnesty records that three 2025 packages were not submitted to parliament. Whether the 11th package was among those withdrawn is not stated.

The February 2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' was reported as excluded from the 12th judicial package; whether it was reintroduced or shelved afterwards is not sourced.

The sources do not document Manisa-level court practice on legal gender recognition, nor the administrative burden or timelines a visitor or resident would face in obtaining recognisable documents.
